beats.role_note: COLD OPEN -- required fellow intro line + AI-voice disclosure; the question
beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Boopesh M., and this video is about the backtest mirage: why an AI that searches thousands of trading strategies always finds one that looks brilliant, then fails on new data. Quick note: this is an AI voice reading my script. And every number comes from my own small experiment, on synthetic noise data.

props.command: Why does an AI that tests 10,000 trading strategies always find a brilliant one?
output: the market: synthetic noise data, so no real edge exists
best backtest Sharpe 1.69 → on new data −0.37
the more you test, the better the luckiest one looks

beats.role_note: BLUF -- hesitant writer corrects the misconception
beats.narration_text: Here's the whole idea in one line. Test enough strategies, and your best backtest isn't skill. It's just the luckiest draw.

props.text: My best backtest proves a real edge.

contextItems.label: Backtest
contextItems.detail: a strategy tested on past data

contextItems.label: The trap
contextItems.detail: test enough, and one looks brilliant by luck

beats.role_note: 7 years of pure-noise prices; 5 years searched, 2 years locked
beats.narration_text: First, a market with nothing to find. I generated seven years of daily returns from pure random noise. Synthetic noise data: no rule can have a real edge. The search may look at the first five years. The last two stay locked away.

beats.role_note: 10,000 rules, histogram of in-sample Sharpe; winner 1.69
beats.narration_text: Now the search. It tries ten thousand simple rules. Each looks at the last few days, and goes long or short. Each gets a Sharpe ratio: return per unit of risk. Above one is usually called good. Most rules land near zero, as they should. But the best of ten thousand scores one point seven. On pure noise.

beats.role_note: winner's equity curve: climbs in-sample, turns down out-of-sample
beats.narration_text: Now unlock the last two years. The winner's line, which climbed for five years, stalls, then slips. Out of sample, its Sharpe is minus point four. The brilliant backtest was a mirage.

beats.role_note: best in-sample Sharpe vs number of rules tried, 200 noise markets
beats.narration_text: Was that one unlucky run? I repeated the whole search on two hundred fresh noise markets. Best of one rule: a Sharpe near zero. Best of ten: point seven. Best of a hundred: one point one. Best of ten thousand: one point six. Out of sample, the winners averaged about zero. The more you test, the better the best looks.

beats.role_note: one formula: Sharpe noise ~ 1/sqrt(years); the paper
beats.narration_text: Why? A Sharpe ratio measured over five years carries noise of about one over the square root of five: point four five. Test many rules, and the winner is simply the one with the luckiest noise. Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado and Zhu called this backtest overfitting, in the Notices of the American Mathematical Society, in 2014. Their warning: with five years of data, about forty-five tries can already reach a Sharpe near one by luck.

beats.role_note: three rules + the bar to beat; honest limits
beats.narration_text: So here's the fix. Count your trials, and report them. Hold out data you never touch until the very end. And demand more as you test more. In my noise markets, one rule beats point eight by luck only one time in twenty. With ten thousand rules, that bar is one point nine, so our one point seven winner fails. Correctly. Limits: synthetic noise, no trading costs, and real markets may hide small real edges.

Your turn. Paste this into Claude, with my script attached. Give the noise market a small real edge, and add trading costs. Does the search find the real edge, or a lucky fake? A good answer shows the numbers.
